scenes.narration: Meet Theo. He's an engineer in an old factory town in Europe, and everyone keeps telling him the same thing. Europe is falling behind. America has the tech giants. China has the factories. Europe has aging towns, pricey energy and a lot of nostalgia. But Theo's town still makes parts for machines the whole world needs, and his sister Nora works on medicines sold around the world. So here's the question Theo is about to chase. What if the technology that seems to threaten Europe could bring it back?

Start with what Theo sees from his window. Europe is not poor. By the IMF's count, the European Union's economy is worth about twenty-one trillion dollars a year, a little bigger than China's. It's a giant. It's just a giant that keeps slipping. Theo's town has a hospital, good schools and a train that mostly runs on time. That's what a rich place looks like.

Slipping how? A report for the European Commission, led by the former central banker Mario Draghi, found the gap between Europe and America has been widening for years. And most of it comes down to a single thing. European workers simply produce less in the same amount of time.
Theo sees it on his own shop floor. The veterans are retiring, and fewer young people walk in. Draghi's report warns that Europe will soon have just two workers for every retiree.

Then there's the power bill. European companies pay two to three times what American companies pay for electricity. And when Europe grows a promising tech startup, it often packs up and moves to America to raise money. Theo's boss has a word for all of this. Squeezed.
So that's the paradox. A rich continent with world-class universities and famous companies, and a future everyone is worried about. Those are the facts. Now comes Theo's hunch.

The old recipe for growth was simple. More workers plus more machines makes more stuff. Europe's industrial revolution ran on it. Theo's great-grandfather worked in this very factory, shoulder to shoulder with hundreds of others. Back then, Europe was the workshop of the world.

Let me draw Theo's problem. Output equals the number of workers, times what each worker produces. If the number of workers starts falling, and in Europe it's about to, there's just a single way to keep growing. Each worker has to produce more.

scenes.narration: So Theo asks the obvious question. What if technology let his factory make far more with far fewer people? Then a shrinking workforce stops being a death sentence. And a different question starts to matter. Theo writes it on the whiteboard in the break room.

Theo visits a modern automated plant. Cameras running AI check every part and guide robot arms. The industry's robot federation calls that kind of machine vision industry-grade. Sensors warn before a motor fails. Self-driving carts move parts. And engineers test the whole line in a digital twin before building it. Theo counts the people on the floor. It doesn't take long.
But the tour guide is honest. Robots that can learn any job are not ready yet. So this isn't a factory with no people. It's a factory where each person does far more. Theo likes the sound of that.
And Europe isn't starting from scratch. Germany already runs more robots per factory worker than America does, and far more than the world average.

Here's the mechanism that changes Theo's thinking. Picture a factory's costs as a stack. Automation shrinks the labor slice. But the machines, the software and the know-how behind them become a bigger part of the bill. So the money starts flowing to whoever owns those things.

Workers don't vanish. Someone designs the robots, writes the code, fixes the line. But if fewer hands are needed, cheap labor matters less, and owning the technology may matter more. And Europe already owns a lot of it. Nora works in the clearest example.

Medicine. Here's a number that surprises most Americans. Last year the EU sold the world about two hundred and fifty billion dollars more medicine than it bought. Its biggest customer? The United States.

Nora walks Theo past the giants. Roche and Novartis in Switzerland. AstraZeneca and GSK in Britain. Sanofi in France. Novo Nordisk in Denmark. Switzerland and Britain are in Europe, but not in the EU. Each of them sells medicine all over the world.

So where does the money in a medicine come from? Let me draw it. Research finds a molecule. Patents protect it. Trials prove it works. Then factories make it, and trucks and planes ship it worldwide. Most of the value sits at the start. In the ideas, the patents and the proof.

Nora's favorite example is Novo Nordisk, the Danish maker of diabetes and obesity drugs. It spends almost eight billion dollars a year on research. It's expanding its factories too. But what it really sells is decades of science that only it controls.

Can AI speed that science up? Nora is cautious. AstraZeneca bought a company called Modella AI to build AI into its cancer research. But a new medicine still takes more than a decade, and for every success, thousands of candidates fail. AI may help pick better bets. It doesn't guarantee a single approval.
And that's Theo's first big lesson. You don't have to make everything at home to capture the value. You have to own, and keep improving, the thing everyone else needs.

Then Nora shows him the most extreme case. ASML, in the Dutch town of Veldhoven, is the only company that makes the machines used to print the world's most advanced chips. Last year it kept almost eleven billion dollars in profit. And it doesn't make a single chip. Theo has to sit down.

It sits in the middle of a web. Thousands of suppliers feed in lenses, lasers and parts. Out go machines to chip factories in Asia and America. Every time anyone builds a factory for AI chips, part of the bill lands in the Netherlands. Nora calls it Europe's quietest superpower.

Theo recognizes the next example. Siemens, from Munich, sells factories their controllers, automation and software, including digital twins. Its chief executive calls industrial AI an exceptional growth opportunity. When the world automates, somebody sells the automation.

And then there's Airbus, run from near Toulouse in France. Its real product is coordination. Thousands of parts from many countries, engineered and certified to fit together, with years of orders already waiting. That's exactly where smarter software and automation could pay off.

Theo stays skeptical. Europe doesn't dominate everything. China installs far more robots, and most cloud and consumer tech is American. But Europe owns capabilities that could gain value as production gets more automated.

Which brings Theo to the big idea. For decades, towns like his competed to host factories and their jobs. In a more automated world, the factory floor may employ fewer people. And the question shifts from who operates the machines to who owns them.

So Theo sketches his own company's future. Call it Company E. Its engineers in Europe develop the technology. It owns the patents and the software, makes the key decisions and carries the big risks. Partner factories in other countries make the product under license.

Now watch the money, with made-up numbers on screen. The partner factory earns a small, steady fee on top of its costs. Company E keeps what's left. Then the factory automates, and its costs fall. Its fee shrinks a little, because it's charged on lower costs. And Company E's share of each sale grows by more than half.

But there are catches. This only works if Company E really does the work, and if prices hold, while rivals automate too. And simply registering a patent somewhere doesn't move the profit. The real work, the people and the decisions have to be there.

So the question for Europe isn't whether it can win back the assembly line. It's whether it can attract and keep the companies, the scientists, the money and the ideas that profit from automated production everywhere. Theo circles that sentence on his sketch.

Then Theo's boss throws in a twist. If robots make labor matter less, other costs matter more. Energy. Money. Logistics. Stability. And the taxes on producing. Brazil, for example, gets most of its electricity from renewables. Yet an industry study found that almost half of what its power companies bill goes to taxes and charges, and the country is now overhauling its sales taxes. So a country with cheap power would still need competitive costs to produce. And even if Company E's partner plant ends up in Brazil, the profit from the technology could still come home to Europe.

scenes.narration: Can Europe pull in the people and the money that kind of company needs? It has real pull. Strong courts, research labs, a huge single market, industrial clusters, and cities people want to live in.
But Nora warns him. Wealthy residents are not the same as productive investment. A head office is not a research lab. Only real activity builds real growth.

And newcomers bring problems. Pricier housing. Wider inequality. Shortages of skilled workers. Rich arrivals don't automatically pay for pensions and hospitals. That depends on what they do and how they're taxed. Nora has watched the rents climb in her own neighborhood.

So what would a comeback take, for Theo's town and for Europe? Let me list it. Let companies grow big without leaving. Make money easier to raise. Bring down energy costs. Actually use AI in everyday factories and offices. And compete hard for talent. Miss these, and the profits flow elsewhere.

So, could AI bring Europe back to power? Not by building the most factories. That race is China's. And not by copying Silicon Valley. But as the owner, developer, financier and licensor of technology the whole world runs on. It's a plausible path, not a promise. Europe has the assets. The rest depends on choices it hasn't made yet.

For generations, economic power meant factories and workers. In a world run more and more by machines, the question may change. Not just who makes the products, but who owns the technology, the machines and the ideas behind them. And for Theo's old factory town, that could be a very different way back into the race.
